definition: Sugar syrup's temperature IS its destiny: thread 110°C (syrups), soft ball 113–116 (fudge, pralines, Italian meringue), firm/hard ball 120–130 (caramels, nougat), soft/hard crack 132–154 (toffee, brittle, spun sugar), then true CARAMEL 160–180°C: sugar itself breaking into hundreds of bitter-sweet compounds, from blond to mahogany to one shade before ruin. Wet caramel (sugar + water) is safer; dry caramel is faster and riskier. Crystallization is the saboteur: don't stir once boiling, brush down stray crystals, or insure with corn syrup/glucose. Add cream and butter and it's sauce; add nothing and stop it dark and it's the top of a crème brûlée's ancestry.

film.watchFor: Chef Taka cuts the vinegar through the rice with the paddle rather than stirring it, so the grains stay whole; the rolling chapter at 7:37 shows the mat tucking and the fingers setting tension.

label: Sweating aromatics: soft, never browned
definition: Three pan verbs distinguished by heat and intent. SWEAT: low heat, a little fat, often a lid or parchment; vegetables soften and release moisture WITHOUT color (the start of risotto, velouté, most braises where onion flavor should be sweet, not roasty). SAUTÉ: medium-high, food 'jumping' (sauter) in a wide pan: light browning, fast cooking, constant motion. SEAR: maximum heat, zero motion: deep crust, Maillard at full roar. Recipes say 'cook the onions' and mean one of three different flavors; knowing which one the dish needs is the difference between following recipes and cooking.

label: Tadka: blooming spices in fat

film.title: Easy Dal Tadka Three Ways | एक दाल तीन तड़के | AWADHI / PUNJABI DAL TADKA | Chef Ranveer Brar
film.watchFor: Three tadkas built in sequence: the order spices enter the hot fat, and the few seconds between fragrant and burnt, seen back to back.

definition: The single technique cluster that separates spice-owners from spice-cooks. TOASTING (dry pan, whole spices, medium heat until fragrant and a shade darker; seconds matter; walk away and start over): drives off moisture, blooms new roasted compounds, and readies seeds for grinding. BLOOMING (spices into hot FAT: the tadka/tarka/chhonk of India, the berbere fry of Ethiopia, the paprika rule of Hungary, the curry-paste split of Thailand): most spice flavor compounds are FAT-soluble, so oil extracts and distributes what water never will; this is why chili crisp works, why raw curry powder tastes dusty, and why the recipe wing's soups start with a fried paste. The sequencing law: hardy spices early into fat; delicate ground spices brief and late (they scorch); finishing blends off-heat entirely. One sentence to keep: spices don't flavor food; fat carries spices, which flavor food.

label: Tempering a custard
query: how to temper eggs custard technique

film.title: How to Make Crème Anglaise (Custard Sauce)
film.watchFor: The thin first ladles of hot milk going into the yolks under constant whisking, then the spoon-back nappe test at the end, which is the only reliable read on 82°C without a thermometer.

definition: One word, two crafts. TEMPERING EGGS: whisking hot liquid gradually into yolks before returning all to the pot, raising their temperature gently so custards (crème anglaise, carbonara's cousin) thicken at 82°C instead of scrambling at 90°C, the thermometer's best friend. TEMPERING CHOCOLATE: melting, cooling, and reheating to precise curves (dark: ~50°→27°→31–32°C) so cocoa butter sets in stable Form V crystals: glossy snap instead of dull bloom. Both are the same discipline wearing different aprons: proteins and fats obey temperature, and the cook who controls degrees controls texture.

label: The bare simmer: holding liquid below the boil

film.title: The Difference Between Boiling And Simmering | Cooking Techniques | Whole Foods Market
film.watchFor: The two pots side by side: the lazy bubbles that break singly at the surface versus the rolling boil, which is the distinction this technique lives or dies on.

definition: Three temperatures pretending to be one method. POACH: 71–82°C, water barely shivering: eggs, fish, chicken breast, anything delicate that violent bubbles would shred. SIMMER: 85–95°C, lazy bubbles: stocks, braises, beans, sauces. BOIL: 100°C rolling: pasta, blanching, potatoes, and almost nothing made of protein. The most common home error is treating these as synonyms; the most common professional discipline is watching the bubbles, not the dial. Salt poaching liquids and courts-bouillons like they are the sauce, because for those minutes they are.

label: The broiler: heat from above
definition: Heat from above: the finisher's station. The SALAMANDER (the pro's open-fronted overhead broiler, named for the fire-myth lizard): gratins bronzed to order, French onion soup's lid (the cheese-pull economy), glazes flashed, plates crisped and reheated seconds before the pass: it runs all service because top-down radiant heat finishes without re-cooking from below. The home BROILER is the same physics behind a worse door: preheat it seriously, rack close, food watched like a rival (the distance-and-attention tool: everything happens in 90-second windows), and use it for the technique wing's brûlée-adjacent jobs: melting, browning meringue, blistering peppers, finishing casseroles, faux-tandoor naan on a screaming steel. The mindset shift that unlocks it: the broiler is not an oven setting; it is an upside-down grill, and once you cook TO it (thin cuts, close racks, flipped once) it becomes the fastest cooking appliance in the house.

label: The brûlée torch

film.title: Claire Saffitz Makes Crème Brûlée & Crème Caramel | Dessert Person
film.watchFor: The flame held at a distance and swept continuously across a thin, even sugar layer rather than parked in one spot, which is the difference between a glass lid and a burnt patch over cold custard.

definition: Directed fire, sold as a dessert toy and worth far more. The canon: CRÈME BRÛLÉE's glass lid (thin sugar, even sweeps, let it cool to glass: the pastry wing's stage-managed caramel), meringue toasting (baked Alaska's peaks, tarte au citron's optional crown). The savory second life: peeling peppers and tomatoes in place, blistering shishitos, finishing sous-vide proteins' edges where the pan can't reach (the crevices of a chicken thigh, a roast's pale corner: torch as detail-sear), melting cheese to order, aburi-style sushi's kissed fat (torched salmon nigiri's entire genre), charring citrus for cocktails. Hardware truth: the tiny culinary torches are underpowered toys; a hardware-store propane or MAP-gas head with a trigger igniter costs less and works properly; hold the flame so food sees the blue cone's TIP, keep it moving, and mind the 'torch taste' (unburned fuel from too-close, too-rich flames: distance and a hot, lean flame prevent it).

label: The coat before the fry: dredge, crumb, batter

film.title: The Standard Breading Process in 3 Easy Steps - Kitchen Conundrums with Thomas Joseph
film.watchFor: The one-wet-hand, one-dry-hand discipline down the flour-egg-crumb line: keeping one hand out of the egg is what stops the crumb from clumping onto your fingers instead of the cutlet, and it is the whole difference between a coat that survives the oil and one that sloughs off.

definition: Frying is violent dehydration: oil at 160–190°C flash-boils surface moisture outward (the bubbles ARE water leaving), creating crust while steam-cooking the interior. Laws: recover temperature between batches (crowding = greasy), match oil to job (neutral high-smoke oils for deep; the double-fry, low then high, for fries, tostones, and chicken that must stay crisp), drain on RACKS not paper (paper steams the base), and salt in the first seconds while the surface is still hot and receptive. Oil is a reusable ingredient: strain it, smell it, retire it when it darkens or foams.

label: The molcajete

film.title: Salsa de Molcajete | Rick Bayless Taco Manual
film.watchFor: Garlic and chiles are crushed to a paste against the stone before anything else goes in, then tomatoes are broken rather than pureed: watch the texture stay ragged, which is what a blender destroys.

definition: The pre-blender that blenders never fully replaced: pounding RUPTURES cells and bruises oils out where blades slice and whip air in: pesto's name is the pestle (hand-pounded pesto is visibly glossier and louder-flavored), Thai curry pastes demand the pound (the recipe wing says so repeatedly), guacamole in a MOLCAJETE (Mexican basalt; season by grinding rice until it runs clean) tastes creamier from crushed-not-chopped alliums, and the SURIBACHI's ridged ceramic grinds sesame for goma-ae like nothing else. The heavy granite Thai mortar is the do-everything choice: spice cracking, aioli, sambal (the ulekan's cousin). Ten minutes of pounding is the honest cost; the return is texture and aroma a machine's heat and aeration subtly flatten. Every serious kitchen keeps one within reach: not for nostalgia, for chemistry.

label: The overnight rest: letting a dish marry
query: why stews taste better the next day
lexiconTerm: The Second Day: Reheating as Technique
definition: Leftovers are not lesser food; they are food at a DIFFERENT STAGE, and reheating is cooking, with its own laws. THE IMPROVERS: braises, stews, curries, chilis, and tomato sauces genuinely gain overnight (flavors marry, fat redistributes, starches settle: the cook-chill entry's 'better the second day', engineered on purpose by restaurants); reheat these GENTLY and add back brightness (the top-note layer dies in the fridge; fresh herbs, a squeeze, a swirl of raw oil resurrect it). THE TECHNIQUES BY FOOD: crisp things re-crisp in DRY heat only (oven or air-fryer at 190°C on a rack: the microwave is where fried chicken goes to become a sponge); pizza in a covered skillet (crisp base, melted top, no sog); rice safely and brilliantly as fried rice (day-old is the SPEC: the chill firms grains for the wok; store it promptly, per the food-safety entry's rules); steak sliced cold or revived low-and-slow then flashed (the reverse sear's little sibling); pasta reborn in a pan with a splash of water rebuilding the emulsion; bread flashed wet into a hot oven for a second first-day. THE ADD-BACK DOCTRINE, the entry's one rule: reheating restores temperature but not TIME'S CASUALTIES: acid, herbs, crunch, and aroma are re-seasonings, not options. Cook once, season twice.

definition: Cakes rise on air you built before the oven. CREAMING: beating butter and sugar until pale: sugar crystals literally cut air pockets into the fat, which chemical leaveners then inflate (butter cakes, cookies where the long cream = lift). FOAMING: whipping eggs (whole: genoise; whites: meringue, angel food, chiffon) into a protein foam, the sponge family's entire structure. label: The tagine

film.title: Cooking Class in La Maison Arabe: Chicken Tagine& Moroccan Salads- CookingWithAlia - Episode 140
film.watchFor: How little liquid goes in at the start, and how the cone returns it: filmed in a Marrakech cooking school with the lid coming off mid-cook.

definition: The oldest cookware still winning on merit: clay heats slowly, radiates gently and evenly, holds warmth to the table, and (unglazed) breathes moisture in a way metal cannot. ROMERTOPF and the clay-baker family steam-roast in their own soaked moisture. The universal laws: no thermal shock (cold clay on high flame = crack: use diffusers, start low), season unglazed clay per maker, and accept the trade: clay is slower, gentler, and serves its own dish hot at the table, cookware and plating in one artifact.

label: The wobble & the skewer: testing a bake
query: how to tell when a bake is done technique
definition: The thermometer is the truth (that entry stands), but the senses are the always-on instruments, and professionals read both. TOUCH: the steak firmness scale (raw = slack cheek, rare = thenar pad relaxed, medium = thumb-to-middle-finger tension, well = tensed; imprecise alone, powerful once calibrated AGAINST your thermometer on your own pans); bread's hollow tap; the fish flake-test at a fork's gentle twist; pasta bitten for the white pinpoint of true al dente; caramel's thread between chilled fingers. SIGHT: the shrimp's C-curl (O means overcooked), milk-solid color in brown butter, the sauce's nappe line, syrup's bubble size tightening as water leaves, the jam's sheet off a cold spoon, proofing's slow-spring poke. SOUND, the most neglected: frying's rolling boil quieting as moisture finishes (silence in the fryer means done or means burning; the pitch tells which), the sear's confident sizzle vs. the crowded pan's steam-hiss, brown butter's foam going quiet ten seconds before ready, the hollow knock of a finished loaf. The pedagogy: use the thermometer to TRAIN the senses: probe, then press, look, and listen, until the instruments agree and your hands carry the calibration to any kitchen with no batteries required.

definition: Flat-metal cooking: dry heat with total contact, no walls, no steam trap. The COMAL (Mexican, carbon steel or clay): tortillas puffed (the recipe wing's flour-tortilla law), chiles and tomatoes charred for salsas (the blister IS the flavor: dry-charring is a technique category), quesadillas sealed. The PLANCHA (Spanish) and TEPPAN (Japanese): restaurant flat-tops delivering full-surface Maillard. Smash burgers' entire physics (maximum crust contact), gambas a la plancha, fried rice at scale. Home translation: a carbon-steel griddle or the cast-iron pan's flat side across two burners; outdoor flat-top grills (the Blackstone era) brought plancha cooking to backyards. The flat-top's professional edge: heat ZONES across one surface, sear left, hold right, the pass's geography in steel.

label: Trussing

film.title: Jacques Pépin Techniques: How To Truss a Chicken for Roasting
film.watchFor: His hands and the single length of string: the legs are drawn in tight against the breast so the bird cooks as one compact shape, and there is no knot-tying fuss to memorise.

definition: FRENCHING: scraping rib bones clean (racks of lamb, tomahawks, crown roasts), pure presentation, honest theater. BUTTERFLYING: splitting a piece horizontally almost through and opening it like a book: even thickness for fast cooking (chicken breasts) or a canvas for stuffing (roulades, porchetta). TYING: butcher's twine at intervals to hold shape. Even cooking, clean slices. SILVERSKIN: the iridescent membrane that never renders; strip it from tenderloins with a knife-tip and a pull. These verbs are where cooking begins before heat exists; a chef who butchers understands the animal a recipe can't teach.

label: Velveting

film.title: Tenderize by 'Velveting': a Skeptic's Guide
film.watchFor: The guide section separates what actually does the work (the alkaline soda on the surface proteins, the starch shield) from the folklore, and shows the oil-blanch and water-blanch side by side.

definition: VELVETING is the Chinese restaurant's tenderness secret: sliced meat coated in egg white, cornstarch, and a little baking soda or wine, rested, then pre-cooked briefly in oil or water; the alkaline soda relaxes surface proteins and the starch jackets in moisture, producing that signature silk in stir-fries. MARINADES, honestly assessed: salt, sugar, and acid work only millimeters deep (oil carries aromatics to the surface); enzyme marinades (pineapple, papaya, yogurt's gentler lactic action) genuinely tenderize but turn meat mushy past their window. Marinades are surface seasoning plus browning chemistry: the flavor is real; the 'penetration' is mostly myth, and the dry brine outperforms for depth.

label: Whipping a meringue

film.watchFor: All three meringues made side by side, so you can compare how the whites behave raw, warmed over water, and hit with hot syrup, and see the difference in gloss and peak stability that follows.

definition: One foam, three temperaments. FRENCH: raw whites whipped with sugar; lightest, least stable, for baking into pavlova shells and folding into batters. SWISS: whites and sugar warmed over a bain-marie to ~70°C then whipped, denser, glossier, safe from grit, the buttercream base. ITALIAN: 118°C sugar syrup streamed into whipping whites: fully cooked, the most stable of all, for torching (baked Alaska, tarte au citron meringuée) and marshmallow work. Universal laws: no trace of yolk fat, a clean bowl, sugar added gradually, and 'stiff peaks' means the tip stands with a slight bow; chalky over-whip is one minute past glory.

label: Wok technique

definition: Wok hei, 'the breath of the wok', is the smoky, singed-air aroma from food and oil vaporizing against carbon steel at extreme heat, micro-charring in mid-toss. The home translation: maximum burner, a carbon-steel wok preheated to smoking, ingredients DRY and cut uniform, everything prepped before ignition (a stir-fry is 90% mise, 10% cooking), small batches, sauces poured down the hot wok wall so they scorch-caramelize on arrival, and the discipline of letting food SIT between tosses to catch char. Crowding is the killer; one portion at a time is the law from char kway teow to pad see ew.
